issues.legal_issue: A will is not established merely by proof of the testator’s signature and attestation when the circumstances of its execution raise well-founded suspicions that the propounder has not dispelled with cogent evidence.
material_facts: The will was made while the testator was in an intensive-care unit, shortly after hospitalisation for serious ailments, and was said to have been drafted and executed there during non-visiting hours.

The appellant, who was the sole beneficiary and executor, took part in arranging the will and had a substantial benefit under it; the will excluded the testator’s wife and other children without giving a clear reason.

The will contained detailed asset and liability schedules, but there was no satisfactory evidence explaining how the information was obtained or showing that the testator had supplied it in the hospital.

The attesting witnesses were associated with the appellant, and the doctor treating the testator was not examined; the evidence concerning the testator’s condition and the circumstances of execution was found unsatisfactory.

The High Court accepted that the testator’s and attesting witnesses’ signatures could be genuine, but found the surrounding circumstances suspicious and the appellant had not removed those suspicions.
issues.conclusion: The appellant did not establish entitlement to probate; proof of signatures and attestation did not overcome the unresolved suspicious circumstances, so the refusal of probate was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 63 and 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, an unprivileged will must be proved in the prescribed manner, including through at least one available and capable attesting witness, and attestation requires animus attestandi. The propounder bears the burden of proving due execution, the testator’s signature, sound disposing mind, and free and informed execution; where well-founded suspicious circumstances exist, the propounder must remove them by sufficient and cogent evidence. A proved signature alone is not necessarily sufficient. The Court relied on Madhukar D. Shende v. Tarabai Shedage, (2002) 2 SCC 85; Sridevi v. Jayaraja Shetty, (2005) 8 SCC 784; H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, AIR 1959 SC 443; Management Committee, T.K. Ghosh’s Academy v. T.C. Palit, AIR 1974 SC 1495; and B. Venkatamuni v. C.J. Ayodhya Ram Singh, 2006 (11) SCALE 148. A defence of fraud, coercion, or undue influence, if raised, places the burden on the caveator.

rule.if: probate_proceeding_for_a_will and propounder_receives_substantial_benefit and execution_surrounded_by_well_founded_suspicion and suspicion_not_removed_by_cogent_evidence

predicates.probate_proceeding_for_a_will: A person seeks probate of a will in a probate proceeding.
predicates.propounder_receives_substantial_benefit: The person seeking probate took a prominent part in the will’s execution and receives a substantial benefit under it.
predicates.execution_surrounded_by_well_founded_sus: The circumstances of the will’s preparation or execution, including its dispositions or the testator’s condition, give sound reason to doubt that it was freely and properly made.
predicates.suspicion_not_removed_by_cogent_evidence: The person seeking probate does not provide sufficient and persuasive evidence to explain or dispel the well-founded doubts.

issues.definition: When a will is offered for probate, a substantial benefit to an involved propounder, together with well-founded doubts that cogent evidence does not dispel, results in refusal of probate.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court should ordinarily not disturb concurrent factual findings when the lower court’s view is reasonable.
material_facts: The Single Judge refused probate after assessing the evidence and finding that the circumstances surrounding execution of the will were suspicious and had not been adequately explained.
The Division Bench affirmed that decision after considering the evidence.
The Supreme Court found no basis to interfere with the concurrent findings and regarded the High Court’s conclusion as a reasonable view of the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the concurrent findings and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: In B. Venkatamuni v. C.J. Ayodhya Ram Singh, 2006 (11) SCALE 148, the Court stated that an appellate court would ordinarily not interfere with a trial judge’s factual finding where the view taken is reasonable. Applying that principle, the Court accepted the concurrent findings of the High Court.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal_from_probate_decisi: The proceeding is an appeal to the Supreme Court from a decision on a request for probate.
predicates.lower_courts_make_concurrent_factual_fin: The lower courts reach the same factual findings after considering the evidence.
predicates.concurrent_view_is_reasonable: The shared factual view is a reasonable assessment of the evidence.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a probate decision, reasonable factual findings shared by the lower courts are ordinarily left undisturbed.
